# Worker concurrency counterexamples

This topic covers process/item-concurrency layouts and worker saturation. Open this topic when equal nominal concurrency or fuller queues hide slower delivery, or adding workers approaches CPU, memory or storage limits.

[Catalog index](../../technique_catalog.md) · [Negative results](../negative_results.md) · {ref}`Compare loader implementations <compare-loader-implementations>`

**`process_concurrency_extremes_negative`: equal total item concurrency did not make worker layouts equivalent**
- Trigger: Loader process count and the number of items each process loads concurrently are tuned as if only their product mattered. For example, two processes × six items and four processes × three items have equal total concurrency but different CPU parallelism and replicated state.
- Attempt: Vary process count and per-process item concurrency while keeping their product fixed. Separate interpreters parallelize Python-heavy work; concurrency inside each process overlaps I/O waits. Too few processes expose serial CPU work, while too many replicate state and thread pools and add coordination, memory and serialization costs. Too little item concurrency exposes I/O latency; too much enlarges the working set and contention.
- Outcome: In one comparison, a low-process/high-item-concurrency layout was much slower than the intermediate control; a high-process/low-item-concurrency layout was slightly slower and substantially more variable. Another sweep omitted mandatory host-to-device transfer, making it diagnostic rather than a valid operating-configuration selection. Too few processes starved that path. In that incomplete-path screen, an intermediate shape led while cold, but more processes became faster once warm, without beating the original baseline. The warm improvement also reached host-memory limits, increased CPU use and storage throttling, and was not selected. Increasing read concurrency at fixed process count recovered part of the warm gain in the diagnostic path. A separate comparison at that read concurrency favored direct over buffered reads. The fewer-process layouts used less peak anonymous memory than the higher-process layout in those comparisons; that comparison does not isolate the memory effect of either knob. Complete-transfer fixed-product comparisons also favored an intermediate process count over a lower one. In a separate complete-transfer comparison, doubling processes while halving read concurrency lost both cold and warm despite fuller queues and slower service at the slowest rank.
- Guards and when to revisit: Sweep joint configurations around a plausible operating point at fixed sample coverage, then confirm the selected shape with longer repeated complete-path runs. Compare step time, slowest-rank queue behavior, all-worker CPU and memory, storage errors and run-to-run variance. Fuller queues can accompany lower delivered throughput; do not select worker layouts or enlarge buffers from occupancy alone. Re-measure after changing execution location rather than generalizing a selected shape to other placements. The best layout depends on local batch size and allocation: a previously adequate layout can starve when local batch doubles. Cold and warm rankings can differ, and pipeline changes move the optimum. No single cause was isolated for every regression. Repeat the sweep when measured-path requirements change, including restoring an omitted transfer. Corrected configurations also hit device out-of-memory, so monitor device memory and retained transfer/prefetch buffers as well as host resources. Preserve deterministic sampling and batch order, but changing process count can still change worker-local augmentation state and assignment; validate model quality. Extra resource use alone is not a rejection gate for a valid faster run that fits its limits.

**`worker_saturation_negative`: adding workers past the CPU or storage knee lengthened tasks**
- Trigger: Input still limits training, and more loader processes or per-stage concurrency are proposed while host CPU, non-reclaimable host memory or shared storage is near its limit. High total memory occupancy alone does not establish saturation.
- Attempt: Add processes or increase the concurrency of individual stages near the host or storage limit.
- Outcome: Doubling processes while halving per-process read concurrency was slower in both cold and partly warmed epochs: slowest-rank load service grew and queues looked fuller while delivered throughput fell. An earlier row-transform concurrency increase slowed the cold epoch and lengthened transform/store latency with more storage throttling, but omitted mandatory host-to-device transfer and therefore cannot select an operating configuration or establish its resource use. Separately, copying the incumbent loader's larger worker count into a new process pool was slower with more CPU use; a smaller default was adopted to limit contention. This compared different loaders, not just different worker counts. In another comparison, increasing workers and pinned slots together yielded only a small speed gain with more host memory and longer lookup/transform tasks as CPU load rose. The lower worker count was retained to limit shared-storage pressure; this was not a worker-only comparison.
- Guards and when to revisit: Prefer a measured increase at the limited stage, such as cache-read concurrency, over replicating whole processes. That preference rests on diagnostic runs that omitted the required host-to-device transfer, where a targeted read-concurrency increase recovered only part of the extra-process throughput; confirm it on the complete path. Revisit worker count with CPU, host/device-memory and storage headroom, using matched complete-path throughput, latency, errors and total resources. Count every rank, worker and native pool. Measure successful completed reads and delivered batches, not submissions or queue fullness. Throttle counts indicate pressure, not an isolated causal delay. Distinguish reclaimable file cache from process/anonymous memory; occupancy alone is not a rejection gate. The no-transfer transform screen stopped after its cold epoch, without warm or accuracy validation; repeat the complete transfer path before drawing performance or resource conclusions. Several corrected concurrency configurations hit rank-local GPU out-of-memory, including the fewest-process configuration. Identical transfer/sink settings implied fixed retained-batch headroom but did not explain the growth; worker-dependent stochastic shapes and allocator high-water growth were suspected, not proved. Monitor per-rank device memory. Worker-count changes alter worker-local random-number assignment, so unchanged sample membership/order is not exact augmented-tensor or quality parity. The smaller default was not fully validated: its cached path still required a rerun and tests were incomplete; a planned uncached-path test could not substitute for that validation. Increasing workers below the saturation point in the same pinned-slot design produced a substantial warm-speed gain; the slot-enabled full-pipeline quality comparison passed. This contrasts with the diminishing return from the next worker-and-slot increase, not proof of a fixed worker limit. Later pipeline changes moved the useful concurrency range. Compare cold and warm cache phases separately instead of assuming equal cache warmth: higher worker counts can trade cold-start time for warm throughput, and in one sweep the warm-throughput choice made the first iterations and a short whole job slower. Do not reject a valid faster run merely for using more resources.
